question: What is the difference between UI and UX design?
reference_points: UX is the overall experience: usability, flow and user satisfaction
UI is the visual and interactive layer: colour, typography, buttons, layout
UI is one part of UX; UX is the broader discipline
Example: styling a button is UI; making sure it helps users finish the task is UX

question: What is the UX design process?
reference_points: User-centred stages: research, define, ideate, design, prototype, test, iterate
Not strictly linear; earlier stages are revisited based on feedback
Decisions are validated with users instead of assumptions
Ends with developer handoff and post-launch evaluation

question: What is user research and why is it important?
reference_points: Understanding user needs, behaviours and pain points through interviews, surveys and observation
Replaces assumptions with evidence
Reveals the real problem before a solution is designed
Even testing with about five users gives valuable insight

question: What is the difference between a wireframe, a mockup and a prototype?
reference_points: Wireframe: low-fidelity structure and layout, no colour or real typography
Mockup: high-fidelity static design with colours, fonts and imagery
Prototype: linked screens that simulate real interactions for testing
Fidelity increases from wireframe to mockup to prototype

question: What is usability testing?
reference_points: Observing real users complete tasks with a product or prototype
Identifies confusion, errors and navigation problems
Measures things like task success and time on task
Findings feed into design iterations

question: What are user personas and why do designers use them?
reference_points: Fictional archetypes built from real research data
Capture goals, behaviours, needs and pain points
Keep the team focused on specific users instead of everyone
Must be research-based, not invented

question: What is information architecture (IA)?
reference_points: Organising and labelling content so users can find it easily
Covers hierarchy, navigation, categorisation and search
Poor IA breaks usability even when the UI looks good
Validated with methods like card sorting and sitemaps

question: What tools do UI/UX designers commonly use and what is each used for?
reference_points: Figma: UI design, prototyping and real-time collaboration
Sketch and Adobe XD: interface design and prototyping
Miro or FigJam: workshops, user flows and affinity mapping
Maze, Hotjar or UserTesting: usability testing and behaviour insights

question: What are the common usability principles in UX design?
reference_points: Clarity and consistency across screens
Simplicity to reduce cognitive load
Feedback on every user action
Error prevention and easy recovery
Learnability and accessibility

question: What is a design system and why is it important?
reference_points: Reusable components, design tokens and usage guidelines
Single source of truth for designers and developers
Improves consistency and speeds up delivery
Examples: Material Design, Apple HIG, IBM Carbon

question: What is card sorting and when would you use it?
reference_points: Participants group content labels into categories
Open sort: users create their own category names
Closed sort: users place items into predefined categories
Used to design or validate navigation and IA

question: What is a user journey map and when would you use one?
reference_points: Visualises the steps a user takes to reach a goal
Layers in thoughts, emotions and pain points per stage
Includes touchpoints outside the product
Used to find drop-off points and opportunities and align teams

question: What is typographic hierarchy and how do you apply it in a UI?
reference_points: Guides the eye from most to least important content
Built with size, weight, colour and spacing
Typically 3 to 4 type styles: headline, body, caption
Supports readability and scannability

question: How do you choose a colour palette for a UI project?
reference_points: Start from brand colours for the primary palette
Add secondary, neutral and semantic colours (success, error, warning)
Check contrast against WCAG AA (4.5:1 for normal text)
Choices tied to context and accessibility, not personal taste

question: What is the 8pt grid system and why do designers use it?
reference_points: All spacing and sizing are multiples of 8 (some teams use a 4pt base)
Gives consistent rhythm and alignment
Scales cleanly across screen densities without blurry rendering
Simplifies designer-developer communication

question: What is responsive design and why is it important?
reference_points: Layouts adapt to different screen sizes and devices
Uses fluid grids, flexible images and breakpoints
Keeps key content accessible on small screens
Improves usability and accessibility across devices

question: What are the key principles of visual design?
reference_points: Balance, contrast, alignment and proximity
Repetition for consistency and visual hierarchy
White space to reduce clutter and aid readability
Applied to guide attention and support usability

question: What is a sitemap?
reference_points: Diagram showing how pages or screens are organised and connected
High-level view of the information architecture
Helps plan navigation and content hierarchy early
Used for communication with stakeholders and developers

question: What makes a UI/UX design accessible?
reference_points: Sufficient colour contrast and readable type
Keyboard navigation and visible focus states
Screen reader support: alt text, headings, labels
Not relying on colour alone to convey meaning
Follows WCAG guidelines

question: What are microinteractions and why do they matter?
reference_points: Small animations or responses to a single action, e.g. a like or toggle
Give instant feedback and communicate system status
Make the interface feel responsive and engaging
Guide users subtly without extra instructions

question: What is Hick's Law and how does it affect design?
reference_points: Decision time grows with the number of choices
Reduce options in menus and screens
Use clear primary calls to action
Group or progressively reveal choices

question: What are Gestalt principles and how are they used in UI design?
reference_points: Describe how people perceive visual elements as groups
Key principles: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity
Used to group related items and create intuitive layouts
Reduces need for explicit borders or labels

question: What is the difference between UI design and graphic design?
reference_points: UI design focuses on interactive digital products and usability
Graphic design covers visual communication across print and digital
UI considers states, interactions and user flows
Both use typography, colour and layout, but goals differ

question: What is an MVP in the context of UX?
reference_points: Product with just enough features to deliver core value
Lets teams test assumptions with real users early
Prioritises essential user needs over nice-to-haves
Iterates based on validated feedback

question: What does design thinking mean and what is the empathise stage?
reference_points: Human-centred, iterative problem-solving approach
Stages: empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test
Empathise means understanding users through interviews and observation
Prevents designing from assumptions

question: How would you conduct a competitive analysis?
reference_points: Select direct and indirect competitors
Compare features, UX, pricing, positioning and audience
Document with screenshots and notes
Identify gaps and opportunities rather than copying

question: What is interaction design?
reference_points: Designing how users interact with a product
Covers flows, controls, animations and feedback
Aims for efficient, intuitive and enjoyable task completion
Closely tied to usability and micro-interactions

question: How do you approach designing for mobile applications?
reference_points: Prioritise essential content and features for small screens
Touch-friendly targets and gestures
Simple, thumb-reachable navigation
Follow platform guidelines and test on real devices

question: How would you explain UX design to a child?
reference_points: Uses a simple, relatable example such as a toy or game
Explains that designers make products easy and fun to use
Mentions talking to users to understand what they want
Clear, concise, jargon-free language

question: What are some common mistakes to avoid in UX design?
reference_points: Designing from assumptions without user research
Ignoring business constraints and stakeholder needs
Overcomplicating interfaces or neglecting accessibility
Skipping usability testing and iteration

question: What are some examples of good UX and what makes them good?
reference_points: Names specific products and explains why they work
Cites clarity, hierarchy, consistency and feedback, not just looks
Connects the design to user goals
Mentions business impact such as conversion or retention

question: How do you create a user persona and what does it include?
reference_points: Based on patterns from real interviews and data
Includes goals, pain points, behaviours and tech comfort level
May include demographics and a representative quote
Validated and updated over time
